questions.question: What is the best definition of a mutagen?
questions.answer: A mutagen is an **agent** (e.g. UV radiation, certain chemicals, some viruses) that causes a mutation. Options A, C and D describe mutations themselves, not the agent that causes them.
options: A change in the structure of DNA
An agent that causes genetic change
The action or process of nucleotide change
The rearrangement of sections of chromosomes and genes

questions.question: Which of the following groups contains organisms that are both eukaryotic and pathogenic?
questions.answer: Fungi are eukaryotes (membrane-bound nucleus and organelles) and many are pathogens (e.g. tinea, *Fusarium*). Bacteria are prokaryotes; prions and viruses are non-cellular.
options: Bacteria
Prions
Fungi
Viruses

questions.question:
The graph shows the production of a hormone during human pregnancy.

Which option correctly identifies the hormone represented in the graph and the labels for each axis?
questions.answer: The hormone is secreted by the (posterior) pituitary and surges only at about 40 weeks, at birth — this is **oxytocin**, which stimulates uterine contractions (progesterone is made by the corpus luteum/placenta throughout pregnancy). Time is the independent variable, so it goes on the $x$-axis and concentration on the $y$-axis.
options: Hormone: oxytocin; $x$-axis: concentration of hormone (mg/100 mL); $y$-axis: time (weeks)
Hormone: progesterone; $x$-axis: concentration of hormone (mg/100 mL); $y$-axis: time (weeks)
Hormone: oxytocin; $x$-axis: time (weeks); $y$-axis: concentration of hormone (mg/100 mL)
Hormone: progesterone; $x$-axis: time (weeks); $y$-axis: concentration of hormone (mg/100 mL)

questions.question: Which option identifies the change in the ciliary muscle, suspensory ligaments and lens when the human eye focuses on a close object?
questions.answer: For near vision (accommodation) the ciliary muscle contracts, which slackens the suspensory ligaments, so the elastic lens becomes thicker and more convex and refracts light more strongly.
options: Ciliary muscle contracts; suspensory ligaments relax; lens becomes thick
Ciliary muscle relaxes; suspensory ligaments contract; lens becomes thick
Ciliary muscle relaxes; suspensory ligaments contract; lens becomes thin
Ciliary muscle contracts; suspensory ligaments relax; lens becomes thin

questions.question: Which response identifies two physical barriers to prevent entry of pathogens?
questions.answer: Skin and cilia physically block or sweep away pathogens. Stomach acid, tears and saliva are chemical barriers; fever and phagocytes are part of the second line of defence.
options: Stomach acid and tears
Skin and cilia
Fever and phagocytes
Stomach acid and saliva

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a physiological adaptation in an endotherm that assists in maintaining homeostasis?
questions.answer: Vasoconstriction is a physiological (internal body function) response that reduces heat loss. B is behavioural, C is structural, and D is behavioural in an ectotherm.
options: Surface blood vessels in a human constrict on a cold day
A kangaroo moves into the shade to keep cool on a hot day
Animals in cold climates have thick fur coats
Lizards lie flat on a rock in the sun to raise their body temperature

questions.question:
The pictures show reproduction in a hydra, a puffball mushroom, a strawberry plant with runners and yeast (not to scale).

Which of the following statements is true about the reproductive process of these organisms?
questions.answer: Hydra (budding), puffball (spores), strawberry (vegetative propagation by runners) and yeast (budding) are all forms of asexual reproduction.
options: They are all showing the release of eggs for fertilisation
All pictures show different forms of sexual reproduction
All pictures show different forms of asexual reproduction
Only the hydra, puffball mushroom and yeast show asexual reproduction

questions.question: Epidemiology is the study of
questions.answer: Epidemiology studies the patterns, causes and effects of health and disease in populations — both infectious and non-infectious diseases.
options: all types of diseases
genetic diseases
infectious diseases
non-infectious diseases

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of direct transmission of a pathogen?
questions.answer: Direct transmission is person-to-person contact (touching, kissing, droplets at close range). A uses a vector, and B and C are indirect (through the environment or a vehicle such as food).
options: Ross River fever transmitted through a mosquito bite
Catching Lyssa virus walking underneath a bat colony
Infection with typhoid through the consumption of contaminated food
Catching influenza through the transfer of droplets from a kiss

questions.question:
Newborn babies receive antibodies in the milk from their mothers. This helps to protect them against pathogens.

This is an example of:
questions.answer: The baby receives ready-made antibodies rather than producing its own, so this is (natural) passive immunity. No memory cells are formed, so the protection is temporary.
options: Active immunity
Passive immunity
Innate immunity
Autoimmunity

questions.question:
The trees of the *Hakea* genus are common in Australia. Their leaves are often reduced to spines.

Which one of the following best explains why this is an adaptation that helps the plant survive in a dry environment?
questions.answer: Reducing leaves to spines greatly reduces the surface area (and number of stomata) exposed, so less water is lost by transpiration.
options: Water is the raw material in photosynthesis. Smaller leaves photosynthesise less, thus conserving water.
The spines make the stems more streamlined, causing rain which falls to run more efficiently down to the roots.
The spines break up the air flow over the stems, increasing evaporation of water from the lenticels.
The much smaller leaves mean a reduction in overall leaf surface area, reducing water loss through evaporation.

questions.question:
A school health screening was conducted in a regional town to identify students with chronic respiratory conditions. The school has 800 students, and the results showed that 56 students had been previously diagnosed with asthma.

What is the prevalence of asthma among students in this school?
questions.answer: Prevalence = existing cases ÷ population $= \dfrac{56}{800} = 0.07 = 7\%$.
options: 0.07 cases per person

questions.question: Which of the following statements about mutations is correct?
questions.answer: Mutations arise spontaneously (e.g. replication errors) and from mutagens such as UV and X-rays. Somatic mutations are not inherited, chromosomal mutations usually have large effects, and most mutations are neutral or harmful.
options: Mutations in somatic cells are always passed onto offspring.
Mutations can occur naturally and can be caused by environmental factors such as high-energy electromagnetic radiation.
Mutations can occur on a large scale and cause chromosomes to be rearranged, but this usually does not cause significant changes in an organism.
Most mutations are beneficial to organisms and result in rapid evolutionary changes.

questions.question:
Three genes A, B and G are arranged along a homologous pair of chromosomes. The figure shows how the chromosomes have misaligned during meiosis and the point at which crossing over occurs.

Which mutation will result from this error?
questions.answer: Because the homologues are misaligned, the crossover points are at different positions on the two chromatids (unequal crossing over). After the exchange one chromosome carries gene B twice (duplication) and the other has lost B — a **deletion of B** on one chromosome.
options: Duplication of gene A and B on one chromosome
Deletion of G on one chromosome
Duplication of A on one chromosome
Deletion of B on one chromosome

questions.question:
The graph shows the smoking death rate (premature deaths attributed to smoking per 100 000 individuals) in 1990 versus 2021 for a number of countries. The dashed line shows where the 1990 and 2021 rates are equal.

Which of the following conclusions can be drawn from the graph?
questions.answer: Most points lie above the dashed line, so their 1990 rate (vertical axis) was higher than their 2021 rate — the rate decreased. Lesotho lies below the line (its rate increased), and the graph shows death rates, not smoking rates.
options: The smoking death rate in most countries decreased from 1990 to 2021.
Lesotho showed the greatest decrease in the smoking death rate from 1990 to 2021.
Nauru and Kiribati showed the highest smoking rates from 1990 to 2021.
The smoking death rate in all countries increased from 1990 to 2021.

questions.question:
Colon cancer is one of the main types of cancer affecting the Australian population. The graph shows the effect of body mass on the relative risk of contracting colon cancer for men and women.

Which of these statements is best supported by these data?
questions.answer: From normal to obese, men's relative risk rises from 1.0 to about 1.75 but women's only to about 1.3. The data cannot show *why* the risk increases (C), and a relative risk of 1.0 does not mean zero risk (D).
options: Gender is not a factor which affects the relative risk of developing colon cancer.
Gaining weight increases the colon cancer risk for men more than it does for women.
The increased risk is most likely due to other health effects of obesity.
Men and women of normal weight are at no risk of developing colon cancer.

questions.question:
Throughout human history, epidemics have resulted in the deaths of many people. For example, the 'Black Death' in the 14th century caused the death of one quarter of the population of Europe.

Which of the following statements is always true of epidemics?
questions.answer: An epidemic is a rapid rise in cases of an infectious disease in a population, which requires easy transmission. The Black Death was caused by a bacterium (*Yersinia pestis*), and epidemics are not limited to winter or to immunised populations.
options: They are caused by virulent viruses.
They occur in populations that have been immunised.
They involve infectious disease that can be transmitted easily.
They always occur in winter when a population has lowered resistance to infection.

questions.question:
A group of Biology students investigated microbes in a variety of water samples taken from a pool, a household tap and a local dam. The students added a few drops of each water sample to different agar plates, taped the lids to the plates and left them in an incubator for 48 hours. The photograph shows one of the agar plates after 48 hours.

Why did the students tape the lids to the agar plates?
questions.answer: Cultured microbes may be pathogenic, so the plates are sealed (and not reopened) as a safety measure to stop the students being exposed to them.
options: It ensured that the students collected reliable data.
It prevented the transmission of potentially pathogenic microbes.
It enabled the plates to be organised more neatly in the incubator.
It prevented heat loss and thus promoted the growth of microbes.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the transmission of a nerve impulse along a neuron?
questions.answer: The impulse is electrical along the axon; at the synapse, neurotransmitters released from the axon terminal diffuse across the gap and stimulate the next neuron.
options: A nerve impulse travels along the axon and neurotransmitters carry it across the synapse.
Nerve impulses are carried by red blood cells through the nervous system.
Nerve impulses only travel towards the cell body and stop at the dendrites.
Electrical signals jump across the synapse from one neuron to another without chemical involvement.

questions.question:
Feather colour in some chickens is controlled by multiple alleles:

| Allele | Phenotype |
|---|---|
| $E$ | Black |
| $E^{\text{R}}$ | Birchen |
| $e^{+}$ | Wild-type |
| $e^{\text{Wh}}$ | Dominant wheaten |
| $e^{\text{b}}$ | Partridge |
| $e^{\text{s}}$ | Speckled |
| $e^{\text{bc}}$ | Buttercup |
| $e^{\text{y}}$ | Recessive wheaten |

The order of dominance of these alleles is $E > E^{\text{R}} > e^{+} > e^{\text{Wh}} > e^{\text{b}} > e^{\text{s}} > e^{\text{bc}} > e^{\text{y}}$.

A rooster with black feathers and a hen with partridge feathers produce some chicks with black feathers, some chicks with partridge feathers and some chicks with buttercup feathers.

Which option identifies possible genotypes of the rooster and the hen?
questions.answer: A buttercup chick must be $e^{\text{bc}}e^{\text{bc}}$ or $e^{\text{bc}}e^{\text{y}}$, so one parent must carry $e^{\text{bc}}$ and the other $e^{\text{bc}}$ or $e^{\text{y}}$. With $Ee^{\text{bc}} \times e^{\text{b}}e^{\text{y}}$ the offspring are $Ee^{\text{b}}$, $Ee^{\text{y}}$ (black), $e^{\text{bc}}e^{\text{b}}$ (partridge) and $e^{\text{bc}}e^{\text{y}}$ (buttercup).
options: Rooster $Ee^{\text{b}}$; hen $e^{\text{b}}e^{\text{bc}}$
Rooster $Ee^{\text{b}}$; hen $e^{\text{b}}e^{\text{y}}$
Rooster $Ee^{\text{bc}}$; hen $e^{\text{b}}e^{\text{b}}$
Rooster $Ee^{\text{bc}}$; hen $e^{\text{b}}e^{\text{y}}$

questions.question:
50 000 years ago cheetah (*Acinonyx jubatus*) populations existed in Africa, Asia, Europe and North America. However, approximately 10 000 years ago, at the end of the last ice age, there was a mass extinction of large mammals and the North American and European populations of cheetahs died out. The number of surviving cheetahs dwindled and today the cheetah is an endangered animal with fewer than 8000 African cheetahs living in the wild and only about 50 Asian cheetahs left.

Explain the process that occurred 10 000 years ago affecting cheetah populations and describe its effect on the gene pool of the surviving cheetahs.
questions.answer:
The mass extinction at the end of the last ice age caused a **population bottleneck** — a form of genetic drift in which a sudden, random event drastically reduces the size of a population. Most cheetahs died, and only a small number survived to reproduce. The survivors carried only a small, random sample of the alleles in the original gene pool, so many alleles were lost regardless of whether they were advantageous.

As a result, the gene pool of today's cheetahs has **very low genetic diversity**: individuals are highly homozygous and genetically similar (inbreeding has continued because populations stayed small). This reduces the species' ability to adapt to environmental change or new diseases and increases the frequency of harmful recessive traits (e.g. low sperm quality), which is part of the reason the cheetah is endangered.

questions.question: For **two different types of pathogen** (e.g. virus, bacterium, protozoan, fungus), name the type of pathogen and describe an adaptation that assists its transmission between hosts.
questions.answer:
| Type of pathogen | Virus (e.g. influenza virus) | Protozoan (e.g. *Plasmodium*, which causes malaria) |
|---|---|---|
| Adaptation that assists transmission | Surface glycoproteins (haemagglutinin) bind to receptors on cells lining the respiratory tract, so the virus replicates there and causes coughing and sneezing. This releases huge numbers of virus particles in droplets that are inhaled by new hosts. | Has a life cycle that uses a mosquito vector. Some parasites in the human's blood develop into gametocytes, which are taken up when an *Anopheles* mosquito feeds; they reproduce in the mosquito and move to its salivary glands, so they are injected into a new human at the next bite. |

Other valid examples: bacteria such as *Vibrio cholerae* have flagella and produce a toxin that causes profuse watery diarrhoea, releasing large numbers of bacteria into water supplies; fungi produce huge numbers of light, resistant spores spread by wind or contact.

*Note: the adaptation must be a feature of the pathogen that helps it spread — not just the mode of transmission or the name of a disease.*

questions.question:
In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur conducted an experiment using flasks with long, curved "swan necks". He filled them with nutrient-rich broth, boiled them to kill any microorganisms and left them exposed to air. The broth remained free from microbial growth unless the neck of the flask was broken or tilted, allowing air-borne particles to enter.

Using the information provided, explain how Louis Pasteur's work contributed to understanding the causes and transmission of infectious disease.
questions.answer:
Boiling the broth killed any microorganisms already present (a sterile starting point). The swan neck let air in but trapped airborne dust and microbes in the bend, so they could not reach the broth. The broth stayed clear, but when the neck was broken or the flask tilted so the broth touched the trapped particles, microbes grew and the broth became cloudy.

- **Causes:** this showed that microbes do not arise by **spontaneous generation** from the broth or air itself; they only come from other microbes. This supported the **germ theory of disease** — that specific microorganisms are the cause of decay and of infectious disease, rather than "bad air" (miasma).
- **Transmission:** it showed that microbes are carried on particles in the air and on contaminated surfaces and materials, and can be passed from one place to another. This led to methods of preventing transmission, such as sterilisation, pasteurisation of food, antiseptic surgery and hygiene.

questions.question:
Opitz–Kaveggia (FG) syndrome is a sex-linked recessive condition caused by a chromosomal mutation known as an inversion mutation on the X chromosome.

With the aid of a diagram, explain what is meant by a chromosomal mutation.
questions.answer:
A **chromosomal mutation** is a large-scale change to the **structure** of a chromosome (a section is deleted, duplicated, inverted or translocated) or to the **number** of chromosomes in a cell (e.g. trisomy). It affects many genes at once, unlike a point mutation, which changes a single nucleotide.

Example — an **inversion** (genes on the chromosome labelled with letters):

| | Gene order |
|---|---|
| Normal chromosome | **P – Q – R – S – T – U – V** |
| After inversion | **P – Q – T – S – R – U – V** |

The segment R–S–T broke off, rotated 180° and reattached, so the order of those genes is reversed.

questions.question:
Opitz–Kaveggia (FG) syndrome is a sex-linked (X-linked) recessive condition.

A married couple want to start a family and are wondering what their chances are of having a child with FG syndrome. Neither the man nor the woman has FG syndrome, but the woman's father had the condition.

Use a Punnett square to determine the chances of the couple having a child with FG syndrome. Show all working.
questions.answer:
Key: $X^{F}$ = normal allele (dominant), $X^{f}$ = FG syndrome allele (recessive).

- Man (unaffected): $X^{F}Y$
- Woman (unaffected, but her affected father passed his only X, $X^{f}$, to her): carrier $X^{F}X^{f}$

| | $X^{F}$ (mother) | $X^{f}$ (mother) |
|---|---|---|
| $X^{F}$ (father) | $X^{F}X^{F}$ — unaffected daughter | $X^{F}X^{f}$ — carrier daughter |
| $Y$ (father) | $X^{F}Y$ — unaffected son | $X^{f}Y$ — **son with FG syndrome** |

Only the genotype $X^{f}Y$ has FG syndrome, so there is a **1 in 4 (25%) chance** of a child having FG syndrome. (This is a 50% chance for each son and 0% for each daughter, although half the daughters would be carriers.)

questions.question:
Lactase is necessary for the digestion of lactose; without this enzyme a person cannot tolerate lactose in their diet. Figure 1 is an mRNA codon table.

The normal lactase enzyme has the following partial DNA sequence (read/template strand):

$$\texttt{C C A T A G C A C G T T A C A}$$

This codes for the amino acid sequence: Gly, Ile, Val, Gln, Cys.

A mutated version of this partial DNA sequence is:

$$\texttt{C C A A A G C A C G T T A C A}$$

For the mutated sequence:
- write the mRNA sequence
- write the amino acid sequence
- identify the type of mutation (deletion, duplication, substitution or insertion)
- state how the mutation affected the amino acid sequence (premature stop signal; one amino acid is changed; one amino acid is added/deleted; all the amino acids change after the mutation).
questions.answer:
| | |
|---|---|
| DNA (read strand) | CCA AAG CAC GTT ACA |
| mRNA | **GGU UUC GUG CAA UGU** |
| Amino acids | **Gly – Phe – Val – Gln – Cys** |
| Type of mutation | **Substitution** (the 4th base, T, has been replaced by A) |
| Effect on the amino acid sequence | **One amino acid is changed** — isoleucine (AUC) is replaced by phenylalanine (UUC); all the others are unchanged |

(The mRNA is complementary to the read strand, with U in place of T, and each codon is translated using the codon table.)

questions.question:
Lactase is necessary for the digestion of lactose; without this enzyme a person cannot tolerate lactose in their diet. Figure 1 is an mRNA codon table.

The normal lactase enzyme has the following partial DNA sequence (read/template strand):

$$\texttt{C C A T A G C A C G T T A C A}$$

This codes for the amino acid sequence: Gly, Ile, Val, Gln, Cys.

In a person with a mutated version of this gene, a substitution changes the amino acid sequence to Gly, **Phe**, Val, Gln, Cys.

Will this person be lactose intolerant? Give a reason.
questions.answer: **Yes.** Replacing isoleucine with phenylalanine changes the primary structure of the lactase enzyme, which can change how it folds and the shape of its active site, so the enzyme can no longer bind and digest lactose.

questions.question:
Panama disease is considered one of the most destructive diseases of banana plants worldwide. It is caused by a soil-borne fungus, *Fusarium oxysporum*. The disease enters the plants through the roots and blocks the vascular system, preventing water and nutrient transport, leading to wilting, yellowing and eventual death of the plant. The fungus survives in the soil for long periods and is spread through contaminated soil, water and plant materials.

The photo shows bananas affected by Panama disease. From the photo, identify a symptom of Panama disease in bananas.
questions.answer: Dark brown/black spots (lesions) on the skin of the bananas. (Also visible: brown, discoloured vascular tissue in the cut stem.)

questions.question:
Panama disease is considered one of the most destructive diseases of banana plants worldwide. It is caused by a soil-borne fungus, *Fusarium oxysporum*. The disease enters the plants through the roots and blocks the vascular system, preventing water and nutrient transport, leading to wilting, yellowing and eventual death of the plant. The fungus survives in the soil for long periods and is spread through contaminated soil, water and plant materials.

Plants do not have complex immune systems in the same way animals do, but they have developed physical and chemical barriers in response to pathogenic infections.

Outline a response that plants have to defend themselves against disease.
questions.answer:
When a pathogen such as *Fusarium* invades the xylem, the plant forms **tyloses** (outgrowths of nearby cells into the vessels) and deposits gums and **callose**, which physically block the vessels and thicken cell walls. This walls off the infected tissue and stops the fungus spreading through the vascular system to the rest of the plant.

(Other valid responses: the hypersensitive response — cells around the infection site deliberately die, depriving the pathogen of living tissue; or the production of antimicrobial chemicals such as phytoalexins that kill or inhibit the pathogen.)

questions.question: Assess the effects of plant diseases on agricultural production in Australia.
questions.answer:
Plant diseases have a **significant negative effect** on Australian agricultural production.

- **Yield and quality:** pathogens damage or kill crops, reducing the amount and quality of produce. For example, Panama disease (Tropical Race 4) kills banana plants by blocking their xylem, and infected farms in Queensland lost their crops; wheat rust reduces grain yield and quality.
- **Economic:** lower yields and unsellable produce reduce farmers' income, while costs rise for fungicides, biosecurity measures, destroying infected plants and replanting with resistant varieties. Disease outbreaks can also lead to trade bans and loss of export markets, which affects the national economy.
- **Long-term land use:** some pathogens persist in the soil for decades (e.g. *Fusarium* spores), so infected land cannot be used for that crop again, permanently reducing production.
- **Social and environmental:** reduced supply raises prices for consumers and threatens jobs and food security in regional communities; heavier chemical use can pollute soil and waterways.

Overall, plant diseases have a severe impact. Because many pathogens cannot be eradicated once established, strict biosecurity and quarantine are essential to protect production.

questions.question:
Cholera is a bacterial disease that causes vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration and death in humans. The diagram shows the five "Fs" of transmission of cholera: fluids, fingers, flies, foods and fields.

Using the diagram, describe procedures that could be employed to prevent the spread of cholera at a local level.
questions.answer:
Cholera is spread by the faecal–oral route, so each procedure aims to stop faeces from an infected person reaching another person's mouth.

- **Fluids:** boil, chlorinate or filter drinking water (or use bottled water), and build proper toilets and sewage systems so faeces do not contaminate water sources. This kills *Vibrio cholerae* or keeps it out of the water, so people do not ingest it.
- **Fingers:** wash hands with soap and clean water after using the toilet and before preparing or eating food. This removes bacteria from the hands before they can be transferred to food or the mouth.
- **Flies:** cover food and water containers, use fly screens and nets, and dispose of faeces and rubbish properly so flies cannot breed or land on waste. This stops flies carrying bacteria from faeces to food.
- **Foods:** wash fruit and vegetables in clean, treated water, cook food thoroughly and eat it while hot. Heat kills the bacteria and washing removes them.
- **Fields:** do not use untreated human waste to fertilise crops, and do not defecate in the open; treat any waste before it is used on land. This prevents crops and run-off water becoming contaminated.

Together these procedures break every route shown in the diagram, so infected people do not pass cholera on to others in the community.

questions.question:
Cholera is a bacterial disease that causes vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration and death in humans. It is spread by the faecal–oral route through contaminated water and food.

Analyse the range of interrelated factors involved in limiting the regional and global spread of cholera.
questions.answer:
A range of interrelated factors limit the regional and global spread of cholera. Firstly, improved water treatment infrastructure ensures access to clean drinking water, which directly reduces the risk of faecal–oral transmission through contaminated fluids. Secondly, effective sanitation systems, such as proper sewage disposal, prevent contamination of water sources and agricultural fields. These systems are often supported by government investment and international aid programs.

Thirdly, public health education campaigns play a critical role by teaching communities about hygiene practices such as handwashing, safe food preparation, and the importance of boiling or treating water. These behavioural changes reduce transmission via fingers and food.

At the regional level, cross-border surveillance systems and rapid response teams help detect and contain outbreaks quickly, especially in refugee camps or disaster zones. Globally, the World Health Organization and NGOs coordinate oral cholera vaccine distribution and monitor outbreaks, providing resources to high-risk areas. All these factors are interconnected; for example, health education increases the community's use of clean water and sanitation, which amplifies the effectiveness of infrastructure investments, and surveillance data directs where vaccines and aid are sent. Together, they form a coordinated effort to reduce the spread of cholera across local, regional and global scales.

questions.question: Draw a flowchart to describe the process of phagocytosis.
questions.answer:
**1. Detection** — a phagocyte (e.g. neutrophil or macrophage) detects chemicals released by the pathogen and damaged cells and moves towards it (chemotaxis); receptors on the phagocyte recognise antigens on the pathogen.

$\downarrow$

**2. Engulfment** — the phagocyte extends pseudopodia around the pathogen and engulfs it, enclosing it in a membrane-bound vesicle (phagosome).

$\downarrow$

**3. Fusion** — lysosomes fuse with the phagosome (forming a phagolysosome).

$\downarrow$

**4. Digestion** — lysosomal enzymes break down the pathogen.

$\downarrow$

**5. Exocytosis / antigen presentation** — debris is released from the cell; in macrophages, fragments of the pathogen's antigens are displayed on the cell surface (MHC II) to activate helper T cells.

questions.question: Explain how phagocytosis protects the body against infection.
questions.answer: Phagocytosis engulfs and destroys pathogens with digestive enzymes before they can multiply, so the pathogen cannot replicate or infect other cells and the infection is stopped before the disease progresses. It is a non-specific (innate) response that acts quickly on any foreign particle, and macrophages also present antigens to helper T cells, triggering the specific (adaptive) immune response.

questions.question:
The diagrams show key stages in the production of gametes and their fusion during fertilisation in sexually reproducing organisms: a DNA molecule before and after being hit by a UV photon (mutation); a $2n$ cell dividing to form four $1n$ cells (meiosis); and sperm cells meeting an egg (fertilisation).

Referring to the diagrams, explain how meiosis, fertilisation and mutation each contribute to genetic variation in sexually reproducing populations. In your answer, include specific references to the processes occurring and evaluate their relative importance in contributing to genetic diversity.
questions.answer:
**Mutation.** The diagram shows a UV photon striking DNA and altering its base sequence (e.g. causing adjacent thymine bases to bond). A mutation is a permanent change in the DNA sequence. It is the **only process that creates new alleles**. If the mutation occurs in a germ-line cell it can be passed to offspring and enter the gene pool. However, mutations are rare, and most are neutral or harmful.

**Meiosis.** The diagram shows one diploid ($2n$) cell dividing twice to produce four genetically different haploid ($1n$) gametes. Variation arises from:
- **crossing over** in prophase I, where non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments, producing new combinations of alleles on each chromosome (recombination);
- **independent assortment** in metaphase I, where each homologous pair lines up randomly, giving $2^{23}$ (about 8.4 million) possible chromosome combinations in human gametes.

Meiosis does not create new alleles, but it reshuffles existing ones so that every gamete is unique.

**Fertilisation.** The diagram shows many sperm surrounding an egg; only one will fuse with it. Which sperm fertilises which egg is random, and the zygote receives one set of chromosomes from each parent. This creates new combinations of alleles from two different individuals: in humans, over $(8.4 \times 10^{6})^2 \approx 7 \times 10^{13}$ possible genotypes from one couple.

**Evaluation.** Mutation is the most **fundamental** source of variation, because without it there would be no new alleles for meiosis and fertilisation to recombine; but it is rare and changes the gene pool slowly. Meiosis and fertilisation together make the **greatest contribution to the variation seen each generation**: every gamete and every offspring is genetically unique, and this happens in every act of sexual reproduction. Overall, the three processes are complementary. Mutation supplies the raw material, while meiosis and fertilisation provide most of the genetic diversity in a population, which allows it to adapt to changing environments.

questions.question:
Type 2 diabetes is a condition in which the body becomes resistant to the normal effects of insulin and gradually loses the capacity to produce enough insulin in the pancreas. There is no cure; the condition is managed through lifestyle modifications and medication.

Figure 1 shows the incidence of type 2 diabetes in Australia, 2000–2021 (number per 100 000 population; A = males, B = females, C = all people). Figure 2 shows the prevalence of type 2 diabetes in 2021 by remoteness area and socioeconomic area, for males, females and all people.

The "Life!" Program was introduced in Australia in 2008 and was aimed at helping Australians reduce the risk of developing type 2 diabetes through group sessions and telephone health coaching. Using data from the graphs, evaluate the effectiveness of this program.
questions.answer:
The "Life!" program **appears to have been effective** in reducing new cases of type 2 diabetes.

Figure 1 shows that incidence peaked in 2008, when the program began, at about 340 new cases per 100 000 people (about 395 for males and 290 for females). It then fell steadily, to about 160 per 100 000 in 2021 (about 185 for males and 135 for females) — less than half the 2008 rate, and below the 2000 level of about 290.

However, the data only show a correlation: the decrease could also be due to other factors, such as other health campaigns, changes in diagnosis or diet. Figure 2 shows that prevalence in 2021 was still high in remote areas (about 5%) and in the most disadvantaged group (about 5%), compared with about 2.5% in the least disadvantaged group. This suggests the program has been less effective in reaching these groups.

questions.question:
Figure 2 shows the prevalence of type 2 diabetes in Australia in 2021, by remoteness area and socioeconomic area, for males (A), females (B) and all people (C).

Compare the prevalence of type 2 diabetes in males and females in major cities and in remote and very remote areas.
questions.answer:
- **Males:** prevalence is lower in major cities (about 4.4%) than in remote and very remote areas (about 5.0%).
- **Females:** prevalence is also lower in major cities (about 3.2%) than in remote and very remote areas (about 5.4%) — a much larger difference than for males.
- **Males vs females:** in major cities, males have a higher prevalence than females (4.4% vs 3.2%). In remote and very remote areas the pattern is reversed, and females have a slightly higher prevalence than males (5.4% vs 5.0%).

questions.question:
In Australia in 2021, the prevalence of type 2 diabetes was lower in major cities (males about 4.4%, females about 3.2%) than in remote and very remote areas (males about 5.0%, females about 5.4%).

Suggest possible reasons for these differences.
questions.answer:
- People in remote areas have less access to health care (GPs, dietitians, diabetes educators and screening programs), so risk factors are less likely to be identified and managed early with preventive action.
- Fresh, healthy food is often more expensive and less available in remote areas, so diets higher in processed, energy-dense foods lead to higher rates of obesity, a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes. (Remote areas also have a higher proportion of socioeconomically disadvantaged people, a group in which Figure 2 shows prevalence is highest.)

questions.question: Describe how a named kidney disorder affects the functioning of the kidney.
questions.answer: **Chronic kidney disease caused by diabetic nephropathy.** Persistently high blood glucose (and high blood pressure) damages the small blood vessels of the **glomeruli**, which thicken and scar. This reduces the kidney's **filtration rate**, so waste products such as **urea** and creatinine are not removed from the blood and build up to toxic levels. Damaged glomeruli also become "leaky", allowing proteins such as albumin to pass into the urine. As nephrons are lost, the kidney can no longer regulate water and salt balance, causing fluid retention (oedema) and high blood pressure, which damages the kidney further.

questions.question: Describe a treatment option available to a patient with kidney disease and evaluate the effectiveness of this treatment to assist with the management of this disorder.
questions.answer:
**Treatment: haemodialysis.** Blood is pumped from the patient's arm (via a surgically created fistula) through a dialyser, an artificial kidney. Inside it, the blood flows past a selectively permeable membrane, with dialysis fluid flowing in the opposite direction (counter-current flow). Small waste molecules such as **urea**, excess salts and water diffuse from the blood into the dialysis fluid down their concentration gradients. Blood cells and proteins are too large to pass through the membrane. The dialysis fluid contains the correct concentrations of glucose and salts, so useful substances are not lost. The cleaned blood is returned to the body. Treatment usually takes about 4 hours, 3 times a week.

**Evaluation.**
- *Benefits:* dialysis replaces the kidney's filtering function, removing nitrogenous wastes and restoring water and salt balance. This relieves symptoms (fatigue, swelling, nausea) and keeps patients with kidney failure alive — without it they would die within weeks. It can be used long-term, or as a bridge while waiting for a transplant, and it does not need a donor.
- *Limitations:* it only partly replaces kidney function (e.g. it does not produce hormones such as erythropoietin), and wastes build up between sessions, so patients must strictly limit fluid, salt and protein intake. It is very time-consuming and greatly disrupts work and lifestyle. There are risks such as infection, blood clots and low blood pressure. It is expensive and less accessible in remote areas, and life expectancy on dialysis remains well below normal.

**Judgement:** haemodialysis is **highly effective as a life-saving way to manage** kidney failure, but it does not cure the disorder and patients' quality of life is reduced. A kidney transplant, where available, is a more effective long-term treatment.

questions.question:
Tim Friede has been "self-immunising" against different types of venom from some of the world's deadliest snakes for nearly 20 years. The process involves milking venom from the snakes and injecting tiny — followed by increasingly larger — doses into his body over months and years, eventually building up immunity to more than a dozen venomous snakes. He has logged 202 snakebites in total. Without that slow build-up over 20 years, bites by most of these snakes would kill him.

Using your knowledge of the human immune response, explain how Tim's body has responded over time to this program of self-immunisation.
questions.answer:
Tim is developing **artificially acquired active immunity**, in the same way a vaccine works.

**Primary response.** The proteins in venom act as foreign **antigens**. After the first tiny injection, an inflammatory response occurs (swelling, redness) and macrophages engulf some of the venom by phagocytosis. Macrophages (and B cells) present the venom antigens on their surface to **helper T cells**, which are activated and release cytokines (e.g. interleukin-2). The cytokines activate the specific **B cells** whose receptors match the venom antigens. These B cells undergo clonal expansion, and most differentiate into **plasma cells**, which secrete specific **antibodies**. The antibodies bind to the venom toxins and neutralise them, and the complexes are removed by phagocytes. Some B cells (and T cells) become long-lived **memory cells**. The primary response is slow and weak, which is why the doses had to be very small at first.

**Secondary responses.** Each later (and larger) injection of the same venom is recognised quickly by the memory B cells. These rapidly divide and form many plasma cells, producing a faster, larger and longer-lasting antibody response. Repeated exposures increase the number of memory cells and the concentration and binding strength of antibodies in his blood.

**Over time.** Because the immune response is specific, the process had to be repeated for each species' venom, so Tim built up memory cells and antibodies for each different venom. When he is now bitten, high levels of circulating antibodies and memory cells neutralise the toxins before they can cause fatal damage — whereas a person without prior exposure would only produce a slow primary response and would die before enough antibodies were made.
